summary: This informational RFC describes a Uniform Resource Name namespace for persistently and uniquely naming resources published by the Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems, the international body that develops space data standards.

plainLanguage.summary: Space agencies write many documents and need permanent names for them. This sets up a naming system so each document keeps the same name forever.

subtitle: Permanent names for space data system standards and documents.

tldr.problem: The Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems publishes many protocol standards and XML schemas that need persistent, globally unique identifiers that remain valid regardless of where documents are physically stored.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7738 registers a formal URN namespace ("ccsds") following the URN syntax rules, allowing CCSDS and the Space Assigned Numbers Authority (SANA) to assign hierarchical identifiers like urn:ccsds:document:313x0y1 without needing to track physical locations.
tldr.outcome: CCSDS documents and XML schemas now have permanent names that organizations can cite in specifications and configurations without depending on a particular web server or repository.

today: RFC 7738 is an Informational specification published in January 2016. It registers the "ccsds" URN namespace with IANA, enabling persistent global naming of CCSDS standards and schemas.

sections.title: CCSDS and Persistent Naming
sections.content:
The Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems (CCSDS) is an international organization formed in 1982 by major space agencies to develop standards for space data systems. It currently includes eleven member agencies (like NASA, ESA, JAXA), twenty-eight observer agencies, and over 100 industrial partners. CCSDS publishes protocol recommendations and XML schemas defining how space systems communicate.

CCSDS documents and the XML schemas they define need persistent, globally unique names that survive document moves, repository changes, and organizational restructuring. A Uniform Resource Name (URN) provides such a name: it identifies a resource by what it is, not where it is located. RFC 7738 registers a formal URN namespace identifier (NID) called "ccsds", enabling CCSDS to assign permanent names to its standards and schemas through the Space Assigned Numbers Authority (SANA), its designate naming authority.
sections.plainLanguage: A big space organization writes standards. They need permanent names for documents so people can refer to them in contracts and other documents without the reference breaking when a website moves.

sections.title: URN Syntax and Namespace Structure
sections.content:
A Uniform Resource Name follows the syntax urn:nid:nss, where nid is the namespace ID and nss is the namespace-specific string. For CCSDS, names follow the pattern urn:ccsds:subnamespace:identifier. The second component, subnamespace, is called the Subnamespace IDentifier (SNID) and distinguishes categories like "document", "schema", or "registry". The third component is a unique identifier within that subnamespace.

An example name is urn:ccsds:document:313x0y1 (a document) or urn:ccsds:schema:ndm:aem (an XML schema). SANA assigns SNIDs, and each SNID has its own assignment process defined by a CCSDS document. The only restriction RFC 7738 enforces is that the SNID part is case-insensitive for comparison purposes; the system must normalize case before checking if two names refer to the same resource.
sections.plainLanguage: Names have three parts: the URN label, a category (like document or schema), and a unique number within that category. SANA hands out new categories and numbers.

sections.title: IANA Registration and Governance
sections.content:
RFC 7738 formally registers "ccsds" as a URN namespace identifier with IANA following RFC 3406 (URN Namespace Definition Mechanisms). The registration occurred on 2015-10-19. The registering organization is the CCSDS Secretariat at NASA's Office of Space Communication. The designated contact is SANA (Space Assigned Numbers Authority), which maintains a public registry of all CCSDS subnamespace identifiers and their assignment procedures at sanaregistry.org.

CCSDS commits to maintaining identifier persistence: resources assigned URNs will remain accessible and retain their names indefinitely. Unique identifier assignment is limited to CCSDS and authorities explicitly designated by CCSDS, following rules specified in this document or in future CCSDS recommendations. The registration also notes that while CCSDS space data systems are openly available, no immediate resolution method exists yet (a Resolution Discovery System), but the namespace design does not preclude future resolution infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: The system is officially registered with the Internet authority (IANA). NASA manages it. SANA keeps the list of who gets to hand out new names.

sections.title: Scope and Community Use
sections.content:
The CCSDS URN namespace covers global scope: URNs are relevant for space agencies' networks both in space and on Earth. Usage includes CCSDS protocol documents, XML schemas, and CCSDS registries. Organizations cite CCSDS standards in specifications, contracts, and implementations. Some space missions are required by their funding agencies to use CCSDS standards, so a permanent, widely-recognized way to refer to those standards avoids ambiguity.

CCSDS maintains public registries of standards and schemas, ensuring organizations can discover which URNs are valid. The decentralized assignment through SANA allows different CCSDS working groups to manage their own subnamespaces while maintaining global uniqueness through the central authority. This supports the vision of space agencies across the world citing and implementing the same standards without depending on any single repository or organization's infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: Astronauts and ground stations all over the world can use the same names for standards. Even if one country's website goes down, the names are still valid everywhere else.

sections.title: Validation and Lexical Rules
sections.content:
Validation of URNs in the CCSDS hierarchy depends on the specific SNID. When a new subnamespace is assigned, the defining CCSDS document specifies how to validate identifiers in that subnamespace. URNs without an assigned SNID are invalid. Reserved characters (%, /, ?, #) should generally be forbidden in the namespace-specific string portion to maintain compatibility with URI standards, but this is a recommendation rather than a requirement.

For lexical equivalence (determining if two URNs refer to the same resource), the SNID part is case-insensitive; systems must normalize case before comparing. The rest of the URI follows general URN character rules as defined in RFC 2141.
sections.plainLanguage: New categories of things (schemas, documents, etc.) can define their own naming rules. The system is case-insensitive when comparing names, so "DOCUMENT" and "document" mean the same thing.
